result.summary: Virgil announces his theme, the wanderings of Æneas and Juno's hatred of the Trojans. Juno has Æolus raise a storm, Neptune calms it, and Æneas lands at Carthage. Jupiter foretells Rome's future to Venus, and Dido welcomes the Trojans and asks Æneas to tell his story.

scenes.title: Invocation and Juno's grudge
scenes.summary: The poet states his theme and asks the Muse why Juno persecutes Æneas. Her love of Carthage and her old grievances drive her to keep the Trojans from Latium.
scenes.stakes: Juno fears Carthage will fall to Trojan descendants and her slighted honour go unavenged.

scenes.title: Juno and Æolus raise storm
scenes.summary: Juno goes to Æolus and bribes him with the nymph Deiopea to wreck the Trojan fleet. The winds burst out and the Trojans are battered, and Æneas despairs.
scenes.stakes: The Trojan fleet and lives are in danger of drowning.

scenes.title: The ships wrecked
scenes.summary: Æneas laments that he did not die at Troy while ships are smashed and sunk.
scenes.stakes: Æneas and his men face drowning.

scenes.title: Neptune calms the sea
scenes.summary: Neptune rebukes the winds, sends them back to Æolus and calms the waters.
scenes.stakes: Neptune's authority over the sea is challenged.

scenes.title: Landing in Libya, hunt and feast
scenes.summary: Æneas reaches a harbour on the Libyan coast with seven ships, kills seven stags and cheers his men while grieving for the lost.
scenes.stakes: The shipwrecked Trojans are hungry, exhausted and without their missing comrades.

scenes.title: Venus pleads; Jupiter prophesies
scenes.summary: Venus complains to Jupiter, who foretells Rome's rise through Ascanius, Romulus and Cæsar, and sends Mercury to soften Dido.
scenes.stakes: Venus fears her son's destiny is abandoned.

scenes.title: Æneas meets Venus in disguise
scenes.summary: Æneas explores with Achates and meets Venus as a huntress, who tells Dido's story and the omen of the swans. She hides them in mist.
scenes.stakes: Æneas is a stranger in an unknown land with a missing fleet.

scenes.title: Carthage, the temple and Ilioneus
scenes.summary: Hidden in mist, Æneas sees Carthage rising and the Trojan war depicted in Juno's temple. Ilioneus and the lost Trojans plead before Dido.
scenes.stakes: The Trojans need shelter and ships, and fear hostility.

scenes.title: Dido welcomes Æneas
scenes.summary: Dido offers the Trojans a home or an escort. The cloud parts and Æneas reveals himself, and she welcomes him and orders a feast.
scenes.stakes: The Trojans' hope of refuge and the reunion of their fleet.

scenes.title: Cupid disguised; the banquet
scenes.summary: Venus sends Cupid in Ascanius's form to inflame Dido while the real boy sleeps. At the feast Dido toasts, Iopas sings, and she asks Æneas to tell his tale.
scenes.stakes: Dido is in danger of fatal passion; Venus fears Juno's treachery.

alias_notes.explanation: Ascanius's new name; he was Ilus while Ilion stood.
Cupid is called her winged Love.
Alternative Roman name used by the translator.

notable_quotes.reason: Famous opening of the Æneid: 'Arms and the man I sing'.
Æneas's line on tears for human fortune, 'sunt lacrimae rerum'.

analysis.text: Fate and divine wrath clash: Æneas must found Rome despite Juno's anger, and the cost of empire is stressed from the start.
Jupiter's prophecy flatters Augustus and presents Roman rule as destined, written under the first emperor.

legacy.text: The opening words 'Arms and the man' became the standard epic opening echoed by later poets such as Milton and Dryden.
Purcell's opera Dido and Æneas (1689) draws on the Carthage story begun here.

fun_facts.text: Virgil is said to have asked on his deathbed that the unfinished Æneid be burned, but Augustus ordered it preserved.

language_notes.text: "Arms and the man I sing" echoes the epic opening; "arms" means war and weapons, the man is Æneas, who is not yet named.
Latian means of Latium, the region of Italy around Rome; Latium is named here as the goal of the journey.
Carthage, founded by emigrants from Tyre in Phoenicia, was later Rome's great rival; Juno favours it above all cities.
The judgment of Paris: Paris, a Trojan prince, judged Venus fairer than Juno, who never forgave the insult.
Ganymede, a Trojan boy, was carried off to be Jove's cupbearer, which Juno resented.
Teucrians are Trojans, named from their ancestor Teucer; "forsooth" is an archaic, sarcastic "indeed".
Pallas (Minerva) punished the Greek Ajax, son of Oïleus, for assaulting Cassandra; his ship was wrecked by her lightning.
Tyrrhene sea is the sea west of Italy; Ilion is Troy, so Ilion's gods are the Trojan household gods.
"Turned his spear" means Æolus used his sceptre-spear to strike open the mountain side that held the winds.
Tydeus' son is Diomedes, the Greek hero who fought Æneas at Troy and nearly killed him; Æneas wishes he had died by his hand.
Æacides is Achilles, grandson of Æacus, who killed Hector. Sarpedon, a Lycian ally of Troy, was killed by Patroclus.
Altars: a ridge of rocks in the sea between Sicily and Africa, called by this name by the Italians.
Syrtes are dangerous shifting sandbanks off the North African coast.
"The brother" is Neptune, brother of Jupiter and of Juno, who is behind the storm.
The broken sentence "ye! whom I—" is aposiopesis: Neptune cuts off his threat to calm the sea first.
Eurus, the east wind, and his fellows live in Æolus' rocky cavern, where Æolus keeps the winds imprisoned.
Haven means a sheltered harbour; the island's sides act as a breakwater against the waves.
"Corn-goddess' armoury" refers to Ceres, goddess of grain; her "armoury" means the tools for preparing bread: millstones, grain and baking implements.
Biremes are ships with two banks of oars; "Phrygian" here means Trojan. "Haply" means perhaps.
Trinacrian means Sicilian (Trinacria, the island's old name). Acestes was a Trojan-descended king there who hosted the fleet.
Scylla was a sea monster beside a narrow strait, and the Cyclops were one-eyed giants; the Trojans passed both earlier in their wanderings.
Latium is the region of Italy where the Trojans are fated to settle; Rome will descend from them.
Ether is the clear upper air, the bright region of the sky where the gods were thought to dwell.
Teucer was an early king of Troy, so 'Teucer's blood' means the Trojan line, from which the Romans were to descend.
Antenor was a Trojan elder who, in later tradition, escaped the sack of Troy and settled in northern Italy.
'Set up a rest for the arms of Troy' means he hung up Trojan weapons as a sign that the fighting was over.
'Planter of gods and men' is an epithet for Jupiter as the father and begetter of gods and men.
Ascanius is also called Iulus, the name from which the Julian family, including Julius Cæsar, claimed descent. Ilus recalls Ilion, another name for Troy.
Ilia, also called Rhea Silvia, was a priestess of Vesta who bore Romulus and Remus to Mars.
'The nation of the gown' refers to the Romans, who wore the toga as their national dress.
The gates of war were the doors of Janus's temple, which were open in wartime and shut in peace.
Harpalyce was a legendary Thracian huntress-princess, so swift she outran horses. The Hebrus is a river of Thrace.
Buskin: a high laced hunting boot; the purple one marks Tyrian fashion.
Agenor was an ancestor of the Phoenician kings; 'Agenor's town' means Carthage, founded by Tyrians.
Byrsa means 'hide' in Greek. The story says Dido bought as much land as a bull's hide could cover, cutting it into thin strips to enclose a hill.
'I trow' is archaic for 'I believe'.
The bird of Jove is the eagle. Venus reads the swans as an omen (augury) of the ships' safety.
'As a goddess only can' means with divine power beyond human skill.
Paphos, on Cyprus, was Venus's chief cult center, famed for incense and flowers.
"Civic din" means the bustle and noise of the city's people at work.
The horse's head dug up at Carthage was Juno's omen, promising a warlike, prosperous nation.
Atreus' sons are Agamemnon and Menelaus, Greek leaders in the Trojan war; Ilion is another name for Troy.
Tydeus' son is Diomedes, who raided Rhesus' camp by night and stole his horses; an oracle said Troy could not fall if they drank of Xanthus.
Pallas (Minerva) favoured the Greeks, so the Trojan women's offering of a robe to her was futile.
Achilles dragged Hector's body round Troy's walls, then ransomed it to Priam for gold.
Hesperia, "western land", is the Greek name for Italy; the Œnotrians were early inhabitants.
Teucrians, Dardans and Trojans all name the same people; Iulus is Æneas' young son, Ascanius.
Teucrians: Trojans, named after their ancestor Teucer, an early king of Troy.
Dido says Carthaginians are not dull or ignorant of Troy, and that the sun does not shine far from them; Punic means Carthaginian, Tyrian refers to their Phoenician origin.
Hesperia is Italy, 'land of the west'; Saturn was said to have ruled there in a golden age. Eryx and Acestes refer to Sicily, where Trojans were kin to the king.
'Would to heaven' expresses a wish: she hopes Æneas himself had been driven here by the same storm.
Parian marble: fine white marble from the island of Paros. 'Enchased' means set in or ornamented with metal.
Danaan: Greek. The Danaans were another name for the Greeks, here the destroyers of Troy.
Simois is a river near Troy; Venus is said to have borne Æneas to Anchises on Mount Ida near it.
Teucer, the Greek archer, was exiled from Salamis by his father and went to Sidon and Cyprus; Belus was Dido's father.
'The wine-god's jovial bounty' is a circumlocution for wine, named for Bacchus.
Helen, Leda's daughter, went to Troy with Paris; her 'unblessed bridal' hints at the disastrous consequences of that union.
The lady of Cythera is Venus, who was linked with the island of Cythera, near which she was said to have come ashore.
"Two-faced" and "double-tongued" refer to the Carthaginians' proverbial treachery; the Romans mocked "Punic faith" as deceit.
Typhœan thunderbolts: Jove's bolts, with which he struck down the giant Typhoeus. Cupid's power is said to exceed even these.
"Brother" because Cupid and Æneas are both sons of Venus. Cupid is her son by another father.
"Vine-god's liquor" is a periphrasis for wine; the vine-god is Bacchus.
"Shorn nap" means towels of cloth with the pile cut short and smooth.
"Light up with fire the gods of the hearth" means keeping the household gods' hearth fires burning, that is, tending the fires.
Acidalian is an epithet of Venus, from the Acidalian spring, said to be sacred to her.
"Unmixed wine" is undiluted; the Greeks and Romans usually mixed wine with water, so this marks a solemn occasion.
Aurora's son is Memnon, king of the Ethiopians, who came to help Troy and was killed by Achilles.

context_notes.text: The Æneid tells how the Trojan survivor Æneas founds the line that leads to Rome; this opening states the theme.
The Muse is a goddess of inspiration, whom epic poets traditionally ask for help in telling their story.
Saturn's daughter is Juno, queen of the gods and wife and sister of Jove.
Æolus is the keeper of the winds, ruling them from a cavern on Jove's authority.
Juno offers a nymph in marriage as payment, a bribe that Æolus accepts.
Neptune is god of the sea. Juno had bribed Æolus to loose the winds against the Trojans, without his consent.
When the universe was divided, Jupiter received the sky, Neptune the sea and Pluto the underworld. The trident is Neptune's emblem.
Cymothoë is a sea nymph and Triton a sea god, a son of Neptune, who helps with a conch shell.
Nymphs were minor female nature spirits, associated with springs, caves and woods.
Achates is Æneas' loyal companion, regularly called faithful; here he supplies the fire and carries the bow.
Venus is Æneas's mother and the goddess of love. She pleads with Jupiter, her father, on her son's behalf.
Cythera is an island sacred to Venus, so 'lady of Cythera' is a title for her.
Juno is hostile to the Trojans and has been persecuting them throughout the book.
Mercury, son of Maia, is the messenger of the gods. Dido is the queen of Carthage, and the Teucrians are the Trojans.
Achates is Æneas's loyal friend and constant companion in the poem.
Sychæus was Dido's husband, a rich Phœnician priest-landowner of Tyre, murdered by Pygmalion.
Æneas carries Troy's household gods (Penates) as sacred symbols of the city he is to refound.
Æneas descends from Jove through Dardanus, hence his claim to a high pedigree; Italy is his fated destination.
Æneas, a homeless exile, envies Carthage's founders because his own city has fallen and his new one is not yet found.
Dido, a Phoenician princess from Sidon and Tyre, fled her brother and founded Carthage; Juno was its patron goddess.
Penthesilea was queen of the Amazons, who fought for Troy and was killed by Achilles.
Diana, goddess of the hunt, was Latona's daughter; she and her nymphs were often pictured dancing on mountains.
Carthage is newly founded, so Dido explains her border guards by the dangers of a young kingdom.
Venus had wrapped Æneas and Achates in a cloud so they could enter Carthage unseen.
Sacrifice to the gods was the proper religious beginning to hospitality and royal feasts.
Ascanius is Æneas' young son, whom he is anxious to keep safe.
Ascanius, also called Iulus, is Æneas's son. In the poem the Romans' Julian family traces its name to him.
Idalia and Cythera were places in Cyprus and near Greece, both sacred to Venus.
Belus was the founder of Dido's royal line, so the cup is a family heirloom.
Jupiter was believed to protect the laws of hospitality, which is why Dido invokes him over guests and hosts.
Iopas is a court singer. Atlas, who held up the sky, is his legendary teacher, which explains his songs on astronomy.
Danaans is another name for the Greeks. The seventh summer marks how long the Trojans have wandered since Troy fell.

literary_notes.text: The poet asks whether gods can feel such long anger, hinting at the story's moral puzzle.
Juno's fear of a future people destroying Carthage points ahead to the Punic Wars between Rome and Carthage.
The poet interrupts with a reflective exclamation on the cost of founding Rome, stressing the epic's scale.
The winds rage at closed doors and the rock roars back, turning natural forces into captive, living beings.
The winds are likened to soldiers in column formation as they rush out, giving them military force.
Pole thunders to pole and all nature threatens death, which magnifies the storm to a cosmic scale.
Æneas' cry to the dead heroes, and his vivid list of Troy's fallen, show his despair and the pull of lost glory.
The sudden "Look!" pulls the reader into the scene as an eyewitness, making the wreck immediate.
Arms, planks and glimmering treasures floating in the abyss turn the Trojans' loss into a concrete picture.
Neptune calming the sea is compared to a respected statesman quieting a rioting mob, linking nature to political order.
The wooded background is a "theatric" scene, comparing the natural harbour to a theatre with a dark stage backdrop.
"True Achates" repeats the fixed praise of his loyalty.
The hope that this suffering will one day be remembered with pleasure looks ahead to the eventual founding of Rome.
Æneas hides his despair behind a hopeful face, showing his burden as a leader who puts his men's morale first.
Venus's questions press Jupiter and imply that Æneas's suffering is undeserved.
Fate is imagined as a book whose hidden pages Jupiter opens, which makes the future seem written and fixed.
Rome's empire is promised without limit or end, exalting Rome and flattering its readers.
Discord is a bound, roaring fiend, which gives vivid form to the idea of war ending.
Mercury's wings are likened to oars as he rows through the sea of air.
The sudden present tense and the 'See!' bring the narrator's voice in and make the divine effect immediate.
Venus's disguise is compared to Harpalyce, vividly conveying a swift, athletic huntress.
Æneas guesses she is a goddess without knowing she is his mother, as he correctly senses divinity.
The terse line shows how brief and terrible the family breach was, defining Pygmalion's ruthlessness.
Venus's question and the exclamation stress the surprise that a woman leads the enterprise.
The swans' playful, triumphant flight is compared to the ships safely reaching harbor, interpreting the omen.
Sensory details of glowing neck, fragrance and flowing robe reveal her divinity as she leaves.
The mist of cloud symbolizes divine protection, shielding the Trojans from all hostile eyes.
The busy Tyrians are compared to bees at summer work, stressing their order, shared purpose and community.
Æneas's despairing questions show that Troy's suffering is known everywhere, a grief now turned strangely into hope.
Vivid visual details of the dragged body and spear tracing lines in dust make Troilus's death pitiful.
Comparing Dido to Diana among her nymphs presents her as a stately, commanding queen.
Æneas and Achates watch hidden in the cloud, knowing more than the others, while the Trojans plead without knowing their leader is near.
Dido asks who could be ignorant of Troy, stressing the fame of its fall and her sympathy.
Æneas' beauty is compared to ivory or silver enchased with gold, showing divine enhancement by Venus.
Æneas promises Dido's fame will last as long as rivers, shadows and stars, an exaggerated vow of gratitude.
Dido's line about learning compassion through suffering foreshadows her tragic bond with Æneas.
Purple coverlets, massy silver and chased gold evoke Carthage's wealth and its long ancestral history.
Juno's hatred is said to scorch like a flame, which suggests Venus's anxious feeling of being burned by it.
Hidden fire and poison hint that Dido's love will be destructive and end in her ruin.
The narrator calls Dido the victim of coming ruin while she innocently admires the boy; we know what she cannot.
The "boy" she fondles is a god who is sitting heavy on her heart, so her tenderness is her undoing.
Effacing Sychæus's name letter by letter pictures Dido's old love as writing slowly being erased.
Dido drinks draughts of love, a metaphor that makes love a drink that intoxicates her like wine.
